key_finding: A nudge that shrouds the credit-card minimum-payment autopay option cuts minimum-only payers by 23% after six months but does not significantly reduce debt, because nudged users set autopay only slightly above the minimum and some drop autopay entirely, raising missed payments.
methodology: Field experiment on live credit card accounts, six-month follow-up, comparing behavior and debt outcomes across nudge arms.
why_it_matters: Directly supports the support team's 'vanity enrolment' worry: a design that changes nominal enrolment/behavior can leave the underlying financial outcome unchanged, which is exactly the amount-vs-enrolment distinction the round-up decision needs settled.
limitations: credit-card debt paydown, not savings accumulation
liquidity-constrained population may not generalize to all app users
relevance_reason: A rigorous consumer-financial field experiment showing a default/nudge can move enrolment numbers without moving the real outcome, the core contradiction the brief asks us to test for.

key_finding: Synthesizes plan-design literature showing automatic enrolment and default investment options lift short-term participation but can carry negative long-term engagement effects.
methodology: Narrative state-of-the-art review of defined-contribution plan design research, abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Gives a recent overview of where the engagement-cost argument against defaults currently stands in the closest analogous literature, useful for framing but not itself new evidence.
limitations: employer-sponsored retirement plans, not a self-directed consumer app
narrative review, no independent effect sizes
relevance_reason: Recent synthesis of the analogous employer-plan literature the brief says is the closest comparator, useful context though the employer mechanism doesn't transfer.

key_finding: Argues default enrolment raises short-term participation but induces long-term passivity: low contribution rates, inactive accounts, and account churn that undercuts the welfare case for enrolment numbers alone.
methodology: Narrative policy commentary, abstract-only, no original data.
why_it_matters: States the support team's counter-argument almost verbatim, but in a retirement-plan frame rather than tested with new data for a liquid consumer product.
limitations: employer-plan retirement setting
opinion/commentary piece with no reported effect sizes
very low citation count, unvetted venue
relevance_reason: Directly voices the disengagement objection to opt-out design, which is the counter-argument the brief asks us to evaluate against evidence.

key_finding: Proposes a taxonomy and framework for when default effects persist or decay downstream, driven by time-course of choice/consumption, antecedent preferences, and trade-off salience.
methodology: Conceptual review synthesizing prior downstream-default-effect studies into a taxonomy and research agenda, abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Gives a structured way to predict and measure whether the round-up default's effect will persist at 6-12 months versus fade, directly shaping what to measure post-launch.
limitations: theoretical synthesis, no new effect-size evidence
not specific to financial products
relevance_reason: The most direct consumer-behavior review of exactly the persistence/downstream-effect question the brief asks about, in a general consumer (not employer) frame.

key_finding: Default rules in Medicare Part D produce large, persistent effects on enrolment and drug utilization for low-income beneficiaries, with passivity remarkably insensitive to how costly the default option is.
methodology: Three natural experiments using random assignment to default options in a government insurance program.
why_it_matters: Strongest available evidence that default persistence and beneficiary passivity are not just a launch artifact and don't self-correct even when the default is a bad fit, a caution for interpreting our own 6-12 month numbers.
limitations: Medicare enrolment for low-income elderly beneficiaries, not a consumer banking app
insurance product, not liquid savings
relevance_reason: Provides a well-identified estimate of how sticky and value-insensitive default effects can be, useful comparator for persistence and welfare risk even though the setting differs.

key_finding: Steady-state saving rates rise only 0.6% of income from automatic enrolment and 0.3% from auto-escalation defaults, far smaller than headline short-run numbers, because of job turnover, withdrawal on separation, and opt-outs from escalation.
methodology: Analysis of nine 401(k) plans incorporating employee turnover, withdrawal, and opt-out dynamics over the medium-to-long run.
why_it_matters: The clearest quantified statement of our support team's objection: the enrolment lift measured at signup shrinks dramatically once withdrawal and disengagement are tracked over time.
limitations: retirement plans rather than liquid consumer savings
employer-mediated enrolment channel
relevance_reason: Contradicts the premise that defaults reliably raise saving in the medium-to-long run, directly bearing on whether opt-out enrolment numbers would be real or vanity.

key_finding: Nationwide auto-enrolment for low-income German employees raised pension participation by 23 percentage points, but most affected individuals actively opted out, and the default effect was stronger when incentives were higher and knowledge of enrolment status was lower.
methodology: Natural experiment using administrative and linked survey data around a nationwide auto-enrolment policy change.
why_it_matters: Shows the default effect's size is highly conditional on incentive salience and awareness, a caution against assuming a flat lift for round-up savings regardless of context.
limitations: public pension system for low-income employees, not a self-directed consumer app
no follow-up on amount saved or 6-12 month persistence reported
relevance_reason: Recent, well-identified estimate of default effect heterogeneity by incentive and awareness, useful comparator even though the pension/government setting differs from the app.

key_finding: Auto-enrolment's participation and contribution gains, replicated at 12 months, are substantially attenuated by 36 months, with modest average savings increases though significantly lower savings inequality; a life-cycle model fits this with a switching cost of about $250.
methodology: Panel data from over 100 US retirement plans and a UK representative panel, complemented by a structural life-cycle consumption-savings model.
why_it_matters: Gives a quantified 12-vs-36-month decay curve for the default effect, directly answering the brief's question of whether enrolment lift persists at 6-12+ months.
limitations: employer retirement plans, not a liquid consumer savings product
structural model estimates depend on model assumptions
relevance_reason: One of the most direct, recent, quantified answers to whether default-driven enrolment gains persist over time, even though the setting is retirement savings.

key_finding: Across three experiments including a 5-country European sample (n=4207), default risk allocations shift investment behavior by medium-to-large effect sizes, but imposing a default (especially one people refuse) significantly lowers how honest and trustworthy the advice is rated, and how a default/question is framed independently shifts the chosen allocation.
methodology: Three behavioral experiments, including a large representative multi-country European sample, manipulating default presence, framing, and refusal.
why_it_matters: Directly tests the EU dark-pattern risk named in the brief: shows that a poorly-framed default can be read as manipulative and damage trust, and that framing of the default (not just its presence) anchors the chosen level.
limitations: wealth-management advice context rather than a round-up savings app
self-reported trust/rating measure, not behavioral persistence
relevance_reason: A European, consumer-facing financial-decision study that speaks directly to both the preset-level anchoring question and the manipulative-default reputational risk the brief flags.

key_finding: Automatic 401(k) enrolment pushed participation above 85% across three firms, but roughly 80% of participants initially accepted both the low default savings rate (2-3%) and conservative default fund, and half still did so after three years.
methodology: Multi-year administrative data from three large firms comparing pre- and post-automatic-enrolment cohorts.
why_it_matters: The classic result establishing that a preset contribution level anchors most participants for years, the foundational evidence the anchoring literature and this project's multiplier-preset question both build on.
limitations: employer-sponsored retirement plan, pre-dates app-based liquid savings
no year given in metadata; older/classic study relative to brief's recency preference
relevance_reason: The foundational anchoring result the later literature (including several other shortlisted papers) is arguing with, directly bearing on whether a preset multiplier will anchor choices.

key_finding: A structural model of 8.6 million taxi tipping decisions finds default adherence arises from the interaction of deviation cost and opt-out cost (84% from their combination), and adding a 15% tip option below an existing 20-25-30% menu captures 69% of the achievable welfare gain at 5.4% revenue cost.
methodology: Structural econometric model estimated on large-scale real transaction data, validated against an independent stated-preference survey.
why_it_matters: Directly informative for the multiplier-menu decision: shows how adding or repositioning preset options in a menu shifts the distribution of chosen levels and welfare, the same structure as choosing among 1x/2x/5x round-up multipliers.
limitations: tipping decisions, not savings contributions
single-market (NYC taxi) dataset
relevance_reason: Explicit method transfer: its friction-decomposition and menu-design counterfactuals map directly onto the preset-multiplier anchoring question the brief asks about.

key_finding: Opt-in short-term savings accounts at five UK firms saw only 0.7% of eligible employees ever activate an account, but among those who did, 96% still had a balance and 87% received an automatic contribution 12 months later.
methodology: Field study of payroll-linked short-term savings account introduction across five UK employers, tracking activation and 12-month persistence.
why_it_matters: The closest available study of opt-in enrolment into a liquid, withdrawable savings product: shows opt-in yields very low take-up but strong persistence among enrollees, a direct data point for the entry-mechanism decision.
limitations: payroll/employer-mediated enrolment channel rather than an app
no comparison to opt-out or active-choice arms
relevance_reason: Studies a liquid short-term savings account (not retirement) under opt-in, the closest product analog to the round-up feature, bearing directly on the entry-design decision.

key_finding: A general theoretical characterization shows that when designer and choosers agree on an activity's value, weighted opt-out minimization is asymptotically optimal, extending prior results that only held under restrictive conditions.
methodology: Theoretical model with asymptotic analysis and numerical simulations, abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Offers a welfare-based decision rule for when minimizing opt-out (i.e., defaulting people in) is normatively justified, relevant to whether opt-out is the ethically defensible choice absent externalities.
limitations: pure theory with no empirical setting or population
assumes designer/chooser agreement on value, an assumption our support team's concerns directly question
relevance_reason: General normative framework for optimal default design that could inform the ethical justification for opt-out, though it is not tested in any consumer setting.

key_finding: Develops a six-category taxonomy of autonomy violations that EU law uses to distinguish acceptable choice-architecture influence from regulable dark patterns, including pre-selected defaults.
methodology: Doctrinal legal analysis and taxonomy-building across EU dark-pattern statutes and case law; abstract-only for empirical specifics.
why_it_matters: Gives the framework for judging whether an opt-out default or a pre-selected multiplier would read as a helpful default or a regulable dark pattern under EU law, directly bearing on the reputational-risk constraint named in the brief.
limitations: normative/legal analysis, no behavioral effect sizes
not specific to financial products or round-up features
relevance_reason: Provides the EU regulatory lens the brief explicitly asks for when weighing whether an enrolment default is helpful vs manipulative.

key_finding: A 12% default contribution rate left 25% of employees unmoved at 12 months (vs ~50% opt-out under lower defaults reported in prior literature), and default-stayers had incomes ~one-third lower than predicted, evidence of strong anchoring, especially among lower-income employees.
methodology: Administrative plan data from a single employer with a high default; abstract-only for statistical detail.
why_it_matters: Directly evidences the anchoring risk in decision 2: a pre-set high multiplier can trap people, especially lower-income users, at a suboptimal level rather than the one they would actively choose.
limitations: employer-sponsored retirement plan, not a consumer app with a trusted-intermediary mechanism absent here
single-employer case study
relevance_reason: Closest available quantitative evidence that a pre-set default level anchors the chosen contribution rate, which is exactly the question behind the multiplier design decision.

key_finding: Title and framing indicate large-scale UK payroll experiments on automating short-term (non-retirement) savings, but the abstract text is truncated and contains no reportable results.
methodology: abstract-only; stated as four large field experiments in the UK.
why_it_matters: If read in full this could speak to whether automatic enrollment works for liquid, short-term savings rather than retirement — closer to the round-up product than most of the literature — but nothing can be concluded from the record as given.
limitations: abstract is garbled/missing, no usable findings
still payroll-mediated, an employer-adjacent channel
relevance_reason: Topically the closest-sounding paper (short-term, non-retirement automatic savings) but the abstract provides no substantive evidence to act on.

key_finding: At-scale UK bank field experiments show automatic enrollment into just-in-time overdraft alerts cut unarranged overdraft charges 17-19% and arranged overdraft charges 4-8%, worth £170-240 million market-wide, though users still captured less than half of available savings.
methodology: Large-scale randomized field experiments at major UK banks, market-wide extrapolation of savings.
why_it_matters: The closest real-world precedent for opt-out enrollment into a consumer bank feature: shows a strong, quantified default effect at scale in the exact self-directed banking setting the brief cares about, and that even successful auto-enrollment leaves substantial unrealized benefit — bears directly on both entry-mode and expectations for the round-up feature.
limitations: outcome is charges avoided, not direct savings-pot enrollment/engagement
UK regulatory context rather than round-up savings specifically
relevance_reason: Consumer-bank, self-directed, at-scale RCT evidence on automatic enrollment into a financial nudge feature — the nearest available analogue to the round-up decision.

key_finding: Auto-enrollment raised pension savings by £32-38/month but was partially offset by £7/month more unsecured debt and higher mortgage balances over 41 months, though loan defaults fell and credit scores rose modestly.
methodology: Large-scale natural experiment from randomized UK auto-enrollment rollout to ~160,000 small employers, 41-month panel.
why_it_matters: Long-horizon evidence that a headline savings-default 'win' can be partly illusory once offsetting financial behavior is measured — directly supports the support team's worry that nominal enrolment gains overstate real benefit.
limitations: employer-mediated pension savings, not a liquid consumer round-up product
debt substitution mechanism may not apply to small round-up sums
relevance_reason: Contradicts the simple 'defaults raise net savings' premise by showing debt offsetting, which the brief explicitly wants tested.

key_finding: Removing an auto-enrollment default and adding a minor enrollment 'ordeal' cut health-insurance enrollment by 33%, disproportionately excluding young, healthy, and disadvantaged people, undermining the efficiency rationale for such frictions.
methodology: Natural experiment around policy change removing auto-enrollment, adverse-selection model.
why_it_matters: Strong distributional evidence that adding friction (the opt-in/active-choice direction) does not neutrally screen people — it disproportionately drops disadvantaged users, which is exactly the 'who is hurt' question the brief asks about entry-mode choice.
limitations: health insurance selection market, not a banking/savings product
ordeal (extra step) is not identical to active choice or full opt-in
relevance_reason: Directly evidences that friction-based enrollment designs create distributional harm, informing the entry-mode trade-off even though the domain differs.

key_finding: Pre-checked recurring-donation defaults raised campaign donations by over $43 million but also increased refund requests by almost $3 million, with the largest impact on smaller, less-experienced donors who did not adjust the amount they gave.
methodology: Staggered difference-in-differences design across political campaign websites that added pre-checked recurring boxes at different times.
why_it_matters: A rigorous, self-directed digital-choice-architecture study showing a strong default effect that simultaneously produces detriment (refunds) concentrated on the least-experienced users — the clearest quantified precedent for the manipulation-risk trade-off the brief is weighing.
limitations: political donations, not a savings/banking product
no multi-month persistence or withdrawal tracking
relevance_reason: Consumer, self-directed digital default study with distributional harm evidence directly analogous to the dark-pattern risk named in the brief.

key_finding: Lab experiments confirm a theoretical model in which a default raises reservation utility (reference effect) and induces self-selection into search, with both effects empirically present.
methodology: Controlled lab search experiments testing a reference-dependent search-theory model.
why_it_matters: Offers a general mechanism (defaults change the search/reservation threshold) but gives no financial, enrollment, or persistence numbers the design decisions could be measured against.
limitations: abstract lab paradigm, not a financial or app-based decision
no consumer, enrollment, or amount-saved outcomes
relevance_reason: General default-theory evidence considered but too far from the concrete enrollment/level decisions to move the design.

key_finding: Mandatory browser choice screens under the EU Digital Markets Act raised Firefox usage 113% on iOS and 12% on Android, with effects persisting from 15 months post-mandate onward, and platform rollout differences (new vs. existing devices) explaining cross-platform gaps.
methodology: Difference-in-differences design around the staggered EU DMA choice-screen mandate on iOS and Android.
why_it_matters: The strongest available real-world evidence that a forced active-choice screen produces large, durable behavior change at OS/app scale under EU consumer-protection rules — the direct precedent for whether forced active choice in onboarding will move outcomes without fading over time.
limitations: browser default, not a financial savings decision
outcome is app usage share, not enrollment/withdrawal amounts
relevance_reason: Named mechanism transfer: forced active-choice screens under EU regulation, with 15-month persistence data, is the closest empirical precedent for the brief's active-choice onboarding question.

key_finding: A usability study of 410 participants found that 'generalizable' active-choice opt-out interfaces (letting one choice apply broadly) slightly reduced granular control but greatly increased perceived non-disruption (98% not disrupted for the best scheme vs a 40-point-lower baseline), while 83% still understood the choice.
methodology: Design and usability testing of nine opt-out interface variants in a browser extension, N=410.
why_it_matters: Gives concrete UI-design lessons for making a forced active-choice onboarding step feel non-disruptive rather than nagging — directly useful if active choice is selected as the entry mode, to avoid the dark-pattern/annoyance failure mode.
limitations: privacy opt-out setting (CCPA/GPC), not a financial product
no enrollment-rate or savings outcome measured
relevance_reason: Names an explicit interface-design mechanism (generalizable, low-disruption active choice) that carries over to designing a non-annoying forced-choice onboarding screen.

key_finding: Opt-out defaults raised sign-up in all cases, but only improved actual effortful task completion (exam participation/passing) for a single exam in the program with stronger implicit endorsement, and only among students who were already responsive to university communication; for many exams there was no effect on completion at all.
methodology: Two field experiments changing university exam sign-up from opt-in to opt-out, tracking sign-up, participation, and passing.
why_it_matters: Directly tests the brief's central worry: that a default moves nominal sign-up but not the effortful behavior that follows, and that the gain concentrates on people who were already engaged — the exact question of whether round-up enrolment will translate into real, sustained saving.
limitations: university exam sign-up, not a financial product
effect depended on program-specific 'endorsement strength', an unmeasured confound for a banking app
relevance_reason: Named mechanism transfer: separates nominal opt-out sign-up from effortful follow-through and shows heterogeneous benefit by responsiveness, precisely the enrollment-vs-engagement distinction the brief asks about.

key_finding: After target-date funds became the default retirement investment option, younger and older workers' stock allocations diverged in line with the TDF glidepath, but contribution rates changed little.
methodology: Account-level panel of millions of US retirement investors, 2006-2018, around the Pension Protection Act default change.
why_it_matters: Shows a default can reshape allocation/level choices via anchoring on the default's structure without moving contribution rates, a data point for whether a preset multiplier would shift level choice.
limitations: employer-sponsored retirement investment allocation, not enrollment or contribution level in a consumer app
outcome is asset allocation, not savings amount
relevance_reason: Weak analogical evidence on default anchoring of a structural (not contribution-level) choice in an employer-plan setting.

key_finding: In a 220-participant RCT, social-norm, framing, positive-narrative, and default-option nudges all significantly *reduced* willingness to contribute to voluntary pension saving relative to a control group, with default options among the strongest backfire effects, and effects varied by income, education, and gender.
methodology: Randomized controlled trial via online survey testing behavioral nudges on voluntary pension contribution decisions in China.
why_it_matters: Direct contradicting evidence against the brief's stated internal premise that 'defaults will lift enrollment' — shows a default option can backfire and reduce willingness to save, with distributional variation by income and education that the brief explicitly wants surfaced.
limitations: hypothetical/survey-based willingness rather than real account behavior
Chinese cultural/institutional context may not generalize to EU consumer banking
small sample (n=220)
relevance_reason: The clearest available contradicting evidence the brief asked for: a default nudge that reduces rather than increases contribution willingness, with heterogeneity by income and education.

key_finding: Representative Australian sample (n=2,100) rates financial nudges positively overall, with strong preference for System-2 (deliberative) interventions and savings-framed messages over spending-framed ones, regardless of whether a bank is the messenger.
methodology: Pre-registered vignette survey experiment, 36 hypothetical financial-intervention scenarios, varying transparency, framing, and System-1/2 targeting; six DVs including manipulation and likelihood-of-use.
why_it_matters: Directly informs whether an opt-out round-up default will read as helpful or manipulative to consumers and how framing (savings vs spending) and messenger (a bank) shift acceptance — evidence for the entry-mechanism and messaging choice.
limitations: hypothetical vignettes, not actual enrolment behaviour
Australian sample, not EU
does not measure actual default effect size or persistence
relevance_reason: Speaks directly to C5's manipulation/acceptance question in a consumer banking-app-relevant framing, which is the reputational risk axis of the entry decision.

key_finding: Offering CCT beneficiaries a choice of bank-account delivery had no average effect on savings, but raised balances for those who started with nonpositive balances.
methodology: Experimental evidence, abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Suggests heterogeneous benefit of account-based saving mechanisms by starting balance, weak analogy to who benefits from a savings pot feature, but the setting (CCT delivery channel choice) is far from consumer round-up enrolment.
limitations: developing-country CCT population, not consumer banking app users
not about enrolment defaults or contribution levels
no persistence data beyond study window
relevance_reason: Distributional heterogeneity finding (who benefits) is tangentially relevant to C5 but the mechanism (delivery channel choice) is not an enrolment default.

key_finding: Abstract fragment discusses liquid emergency-savings funds tied to an automatic IRA design, with contribution amounts equal across compared cases.
methodology: abstract-only, appears to be a policy/program comparison report.
why_it_matters: Touches the liquid-savings-plus-auto-enrolment combination relevant to a round-up pot, but the abstract gives no usable effect sizes or design detail.
limitations: abstract too truncated/garbled to extract findings
IRA/retirement framing, not a consumer app
no clear effect size or persistence data
relevance_reason: Nominally on-topic (auto-enrolment plus liquid savings) but the abstract does not supply anything decision-useful.

key_finding: Switching a 401(k) plan from opt-in to automatic enrolment (opt-out) dramatically raised participation, and most enrollees stuck to the default contribution rate and default fund allocation even years later.
methodology: Before/after natural experiment on one large US corporation's 401(k) records.
why_it_matters: The foundational demonstration that defaults both raise enrolment and anchor the level chosen — the literature every later default study (including this brief's question) argues with, though the mechanism runs through employer-set defaults.
limitations: employer-mediated retirement plan, not a consumer app
locked, illiquid savings vehicle, unlike a round-up pot
over two decades old, predates current fintech/regulatory climate
relevance_reason: Closest classic precedent for both the default-effect-size and anchoring questions, cited as the reason the brief wants more recent, consumer-context evidence.

key_finding: Compares savings behaviours between automatically enrolled and voluntarily enrolled participants in a defined contribution plan (no abstract available to state direction or magnitude).
methodology: abstract-only; likely observational comparison of DC plan cohorts.
why_it_matters: Potentially a recent auto- vs voluntary-enrolment comparison, but with no abstract the paper cannot be used to update any of the brief's specific effect-size or persistence questions.
limitations: no abstract provided, so findings and effect sizes are unknown
defined contribution retirement plan setting, not a consumer app
employer-mediated by nature of DC plans
relevance_reason: Title matches the core enrolment-design question but lack of abstract content limits its use.

key_finding: Institutional mistrust and minority status predict both under-saving and early withdrawal of retirement savings, identifying a 'double jeopardy' group harmed by both low saving and early cash-out following a pension-freedom reform.
methodology: Analysis of three representative Estonian surveys (2020-2022) around a policy reform introducing an early-withdrawal option.
why_it_matters: Directly bears on the support team's concern that passively-enrolled, low-trust users are the ones who withdraw early — a heterogeneity finding the brief explicitly asks for (who is helped, who is hurt).
limitations: mandatory pension savings context, not a self-directed liquid consumer product
correlational survey data, not causal identification of default effects
Estonian institutional-trust context may not generalise
relevance_reason: Gives a distributional/heterogeneity finding on exactly the withdrawal-and-mistrust dynamic the brief's support team worries about.

key_finding: In a 24,303-respondent G7 survey experiment, prompting people to reflect on default (automatic) enrolment into a booster policy reduced stated vaccination intentions and policy approval rather than increasing them.
methodology: Large-scale online survey experiment across G7 countries manipulating reflection on a hypothetical default-enrolment nudge.
why_it_matters: Direct evidence that surfacing a default to users can trigger backlash and reduced buy-in — cautions against assuming a default silently and passively raises uptake without inviting scrutiny, relevant to the manipulation/reputational-risk question.
limitations: vaccination/public-health domain, not financial saving
hypothetical policy, not observed enrolment behaviour
no measure of actual behavioural default effect, only stated intentions
relevance_reason: Contradicts the 'defaults always help, and passively' premise by showing reflection on a default can backfire — evidence the transparency/manipulation risk cuts both ways.

key_finding: Among US Millennials, automatic enrolment and employer matching contributions are associated with higher likelihood of retirement plan participation; their absence is a key reason for non-participation.
methodology: Cross-sectional analysis of the 2018 FINRA Millennial Investment Study, controlling for debt, income, risk tolerance, and assets.
why_it_matters: Reconfirms the well-established default-enrolment participation lift in a younger cohort, but adds little beyond what the classic 401(k) literature already establishes and is purely correlational.
limitations: employer-sponsored retirement plans, not a consumer app
correlational, not causal
no persistence, amount-saved, or anchoring measures
relevance_reason: Adds a recent demographic replication of the default-participation link but does not move any of the brief's open questions beyond prior work.

key_finding: Using 41 million Danish observations, automatic (passive) employer contributions raise total wealth accumulation substantially, while active-choice tax subsidies mostly just shift assets across accounts (each $1 of subsidy raises saving by only 1 cent); ~85% of people are 'passive savers' unresponsive to subsidies but moved by automatic contributions.
methodology: Large-scale administrative panel data analysis, Denmark, distinguishing active vs passive responses to retirement savings policies.
why_it_matters: The strongest available evidence that passive/default mechanisms change real savings amounts (not just nominal enrolment) while active-choice incentives mostly reshuffle existing assets — central to the brief's 'does the default change the amount saved' question, though the mechanism here is employer/tax-driven.
limitations: Danish pension/tax-account system, not a liquid consumer app
active vs passive here means subsidy response, not opt-in/opt-out/active-choice onboarding
no equivalent measure of short-term withdrawal or disengagement
relevance_reason: Landmark quantification of passive vs active savings responses and crowd-out, the estimate the current literature on default effectiveness measures itself against.

key_finding: Introduces and field-tests 'active choice' and an 'enhanced active choice' variant (highlighting losses from the non-preferred option) as alternatives to automatic enrolment when opt-out defaults are infeasible or ethically fraught.
methodology: Review of prior active-choice literature (Carroll, Choi, Laibson, Madrian, Metrick) plus original field experiments testing active choice and enhanced active choice.
why_it_matters: This is the origin of the 'active choice' design the brief is directly weighing against opt-in/opt-out; the enhanced active-choice mechanism (framing the forgone option as a loss) is a concrete, transferable technique for the onboarding screen regardless of the medication-adherence setting it was tested in.
limitations: primary tests were in health/medication-adherence settings, not financial products
does not report enrolment-persistence or amount-saved outcomes
abstract gives no numeric effect sizes
relevance_reason: Names and tests the exact active-choice / enhanced active-choice mechanism the brief is deciding between for the entry design — an explicit design transfer regardless of the health-domain testbed.

key_finding: A comprehensive overview of behavioural household finance covering consumption/savings, borrowing, payments, and the interventions (choice architecture, product design, defaults, disclosure) firms and governments use to shape financial behaviour.
methodology: Narrative review/book chapter synthesising the behavioural household finance literature; abstract-only detail on specific effect sizes.
why_it_matters: Provides the broad synthesis of choice-architecture evidence (including but not limited to defaults) that situates the brief's specific enrolment/level decisions within the wider behavioural toolkit, useful for identifying what else (framing, disclosure) might substitute for or complement a default.
limitations: broad synthesis, not a source of new effect sizes for this specific product
covers both employer and consumer settings without isolating the difference the brief cares about
abstract gives no numbers
relevance_reason: Satisfies the brief's need for at least one review/meta-analysis giving synthesised evidence on choice-architecture effects across financial contexts.

key_finding: Automatic enrolment pushed 401(k) participation above 85% at three firms, but about 80% of participants initially accepted both the low default savings rate and conservative default fund, and half still did so after three years; net effect on wealth accumulation was roughly a wash on average but reduced non-participation in the lower tail.
methodology: Multi-year administrative panel data from three large US firms before/after automatic enrolment adoption.
why_it_matters: Gives precise persistence numbers (half still at default after three years) and shows a pre-set level can anchor contributions in a way that offsets the participation gain — the clearest quantified precedent for the anchoring risk in choosing which round-up multiplier to pre-select.
limitations: employer-sponsored 401(k) plans, illiquid, unlike a round-up savings pot
over two decades old, before current fintech/regulatory norms
no consumer self-directed comparison
relevance_reason: The most quantitatively precise foundational precedent for both the persistence (C2) and anchoring (C3) questions, even though the setting is an employer plan.

key_finding: A randomized field experiment in Afghanistan found default enrolment into a salary-linked savings account raised participation by 40 percentage points (equivalent to a 50% match), driven by present bias and the cognitive cost of choosing, and also increased subsequent active/voluntary saving after the study ended.
methodology: Randomized controlled trial randomly assigning employees to different default savings-account configurations, with follow-on interventions isolating mechanisms.
why_it_matters: One of the few RCTs to causally decompose why defaults work and to show the default effect persisted into subsequent voluntary behaviour rather than just at initial enrolment — directly relevant to whether the brief's default would produce lasting engagement or just nominal sign-up.
limitations: salary-linked account tied to an employer, not a self-directed consumer app
developing-country context very different from EU fintech regulatory environment
no anchoring-on-level or active-choice comparison
relevance_reason: Strongest causal RCT evidence on default effect size and mechanism, with rare evidence that the effect persists into subsequent voluntary saving behaviour.

key_finding: A field experiment with a Brazilian financial-management platform found payment reminders cut credit-card late fees by 14% but raised overdraft fees by 9%, with users who had a history of overdraft use experiencing a net 5% increase in total fees while everyone else saved 15%.
methodology: Randomized field experiment on a consumer financial-management platform in Brazil; fee outcomes tracked across credit card and checking accounts.
why_it_matters: Directly evidences the brief's concern that a nudge can help most users while quietly harming a subgroup, exactly the heterogeneity risk the team must check before defaulting everyone into round-up savings; it argues for segmenting who gets defaulted in rather than assuming a uniform benefit.
limitations: studies payment reminders, not enrolment defaults or preset contribution levels
Brazilian credit/overdraft context rather than EU round-up savings
no data on persistence beyond the fee-outcome window reported in the abstract
relevance_reason: Provides a rigorous, consumer-financial (non-employer) RCT showing that a nudge's average benefit conceals harm to a subgroup, the strongest available evidence on the brief's distributional/manipulation-risk question (C5).
